I have been working this land for forty years. My body knows the seasons before the calendar tells me. My husband and I are only two now, so I cannot take on more than we can handle together. I am getting older but I know this soil — the sandy loam here in Quzhou, how it drains, how it holds heat.

I will split the land the way I always do. Eight mu for the wheat and maize rotation — that is my main food and income. Four mu for cotton — cotton brings cash money when the price is good, and I have grown it my whole life. I know how to read the bolls.

For **wheat**, I rotary till after the maize comes off in late September. I apply the base fertilizer then — diammonium phosphate and urea mixed together, the way I learned from my neighbors decades ago. I plant in mid-October with the hand-pushed seeder my son helped me buy. I water at planting, at jointing in March, and at heading in April. If it is dry in May I water again at grain filling. I spray once for aphids and once for powdery mildew in spring. I use the improved Jimai variety seed I buy from the village shop — not the old ones I saved myself, those yields were too low.

For **maize**, I plant right behind the wheat combine in June. No time to till — I drill the hybrid seed directly into the stubble. My son told me this saves water and the stalks protect the soil. I top-dress urea when the plants are knee-high. I irrigate twice if the summer rains do not come. Maize here mostly takes care of itself compared to cotton.

For **cotton**, I plough deep in April, work in manure and base fertilizer. I plant in late April or early May. Cotton drinks water and needs watching — I irrigate four times through the season, more if August is hot and dry. I spray five or six times for insects. The Bt seed I use now means fewer sprays for bollworm than before, but aphids and spider mites still come. Cotton is hard work but I know it.
